paragraphs.text: Anthropic began rolling out a beta feature called "Install as app" on November 24, 2026, which lets people turn artifacts made in Claude into standalone apps for Mac and Windows. According to the company's announcement, an installed artifact gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude, and it can still use Claude and the connectors a user has set up.

The feature is rolling out on all plans, Anthropic said. TestingCatalog lists them as Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise. On Team plans it is on by default, while Enterprise organizations need an owner to switch it on. Organizations with HIPAA-ready setups and hybrid deployments cannot use it.

Anthropic's instructions are short: update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact, and choose Install as app from the Share menu. TestingCatalog reports that the option also appears in the artifact's title menu and in a right-click menu, and that it requires desktop version 6.28899.0 or later, citing Anthropic's help center. There is no separate packaging or signing step and no API key, and users must be online and signed in to Claude to open an installed app.

On a Mac, installed apps go into a Claude Apps folder inside the user's Applications folder, according to TestingCatalog, while on Windows they appear in the Start menu or as a desktop shortcut. The Next Web reports that the feature is not available on Linux, on the web or on mobile. Claude Docs, Slides and Sheets, legacy artifacts and live artifacts from Claude Cowork cannot be installed, TestingCatalog said.
When the underlying artifact is edited, the installed app updates automatically. Requests that an app sends to Claude count toward the user's plan usage limits, according to Anthropic.

Anthropic describes three levels of access. By default, an installed app can only do what it could do in a web browser. With app permissions, it can ask for features the company says Claude can tightly control, such as sending notifications, adding a menu bar or system tray item, keeping a window on top of others and listening for global keyboard shortcuts. The highest level, full computer access, lets an app ask to run programs and to read, change or delete files without asking each time.

Full computer access is limited to apps the user made, or on Team and Enterprise plans to apps made by people in the same organization, and admins on those plans can turn app permissions and full access on or off. Anthropic states that it does not review apps before they are installed and advises granting full access only to apps the user trusts. A permission covers only the current version of an app, so Claude asks again after every update, though parts of an app loaded from another website can change without a new request. The Next Web adds that zero data retention does not apply to these apps.

Anthropic showed demo apps built by its staff, including a menu bar and tray app called Vitals for checking a computer's performance. Anthropic engineer Felix Rieseberg wrote on X that he had used the feature to build his own terminals, file managers, video editors, communication tools and desktop pets, according to TestingCatalog.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the update moves Claude artifacts from throwaway previews toward small personal software that people keep using. It also shifts a security decision onto users: an app built in a chat can now ask to run programs and delete files, and the protection rests on the permission prompts and on users only trusting apps they or their colleagues made.
Watch whether Enterprise owners switch the feature on and whether they allow full computer access, and whether Anthropic extends installed apps beyond Mac and Windows when the beta ends.
